newsitem.title: FRANCE: Talks resume, French truckers raise stakes.
newsitem.headline: Talks resume, French truckers raise stakes.

text.p: Talks resumed on Friday between French haulage bosses and truckers who stepped up protests by blockading roads for a fifth day and sealing off more petrol depots around the country.

Unionists were cautiously optimistic that a solution could be found on their demands for wage hikes and shorter working hours but said the next 48 hours would be crucial as the protests showed the first signs of hurting the economy.
Haulage companies said in a statement they agreed to one of the truckers' demand to be paid for all working hours, including time spent for loading rather than behind the wheel.
Wary of a conflict recalling a crippling 24-day rail strike last year, the government bowed to a demand from the unions and sent a Transport Ministry official to chair the talks.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe called on both sides to end the dispute rapidly because road haulage was crucial to the economy.

"A solution must be found through talks between haulage bosses and their employees," he said, appearently rejecting demands that the government agree to co-finance retirement at 55 instead of 60 for drivers.
Truckers have singled out Bordeaux, where Juppe is the mayor, blocking accesses to the southwestern city. Petrol stations in the city ran out of fuel.
Paris has been relatively spared so far, but truckers blocked a motorway to the capital's giant wholesale food market at Rungis. Police said food was still getting through.
Protesters had blocked or snarled traffic on some accesses to Paris for an hour after an earlier round of talks broke off in the small hours.

In the Mediterranean port of Marseille, unions urged truckers to make for the capital. Nicole Notat, leader of France's biggest union, the pro-Socialist CFDT, threatened to call a demonstration in the capital for Monday if talks failed.
About 50,000 trucks were taking part in the protests according to unions, and the drivers were bent on continuing their action until their demands were met.

Truckers blockaded a dozen petrol depots and refineries, threatening a supply shortage soon. Lorries blocked the Lille-Paris motorway near Lille and 15 lorries prevented tanks at the Donges refinery near Saint-Nazaire from being filled.

After blockading depots in Bordeaux and Caen, lorries also sealed off depots in Lyon, Fos-sur-Mer, Lacq and Frontignan. Two other refineries in the Bouches-du-Rhone and the Marseille region were also closed off.

Motorways in and out of 30 towns and cities across the country were blocked by trucks, recalling a 1992 truckers' blockade that paralysed France in a protest against a new points system for driving licences.
Toulouse, Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand, Caen, Le Mans and the Franco-German border at Strasbourg were among the hardest hit.

Unions said earlier they might blockade the capital but only as a last resort. "Blockades are more efficient 150 kms away (90 miles) from Paris rather than just around the city," said one official who took part in the negotiations.
The government is wary of taking a soft stance as several big companies including car-makers Renault and PSA Peugeot Citroen want its approval for plans to lay off workers at 55.
Brigitte Bardot, film goddess turned animal rights activist, urged veterinary services to ensure that animals stranded in the trucks in cold weather were fed and given water.
"I respect the truckers' grievances but I ask them not to let the animals, who are at the heart of the conflict, die," she said.
